reason: The source line says opening line and that is false: the quotation is the opening sentence, and the opening line runs past it. The reprint the verifier cites, which carries the permission credit Now I Become Myself by May Sarton, from Collected Poems 1930-1993, W. W. Norton, 1993, prints the poem as Now I become myself. It's taken / Time, many years and places; / I have been dissolved and shaken, / Worn other people's faces. Line 1 is Now I become myself. It's taken. So the card would print a locator the book contradicts, and the honest thing the note already half says (the poem's first sentence ends where the quotation ends) belongs in the source. That alone is the refutation and it is cheap to fix. Two further weaknesses the editor should weigh. The evidence is a blog's reprint, not the named Norton volume; the credit line makes the edition claim reasonable but nobody opened Collected Poems 1930 to 1993, and the note's admission that the 1974 Collected Poems 1930 to 1973 was not opened does not cover that. And four words identical to the poem's own title make a card that cites itself, with no counsel in it, which is a thin fit for a month of maxims and advice. What does hold: Sarton is not banned, not at cap, not shipped and opens like nothing shipped (shipped.js clean); the poem is of 1953, well before 2000; Poetry is the form; the quotation ends in a full stop and uses no straight double quote; the source leads with the name, carries no dash and is inside 140; a fragment shorter than one line needs no slash, so rule 7 is not breached by the absence of a break, only by the word line in the locator.
betterCitation: May Sarton, Now I Become Myself, line 1, first sentence only, Collected Poems 1930 to 1993 (W. W. Norton, 1993)
